source.citation: John Ford Barbour, article on cerebro-spinal concussion, Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 18 (1891): 147–148. Title to confirm from the page image.

inferred: setting (City Hospital; the author saw her there)

complaints: pain in the back, and pain all over the body
vague pains in the trunk and legs
presentation.course: Her dress caught as she left a street car, and she fell on her lower back. She felt little at first; months later the spinal symptoms began and grew steadily worse.

findings: no deformity of the back; pain wherever touched
later: loss of knee reflex, pupils that do not react to light, girdle pain, lightning pains
a spastic element; double vision in her last weeks
periodDiagnosis: at first taken for hysteria or spinal concussion; finally locomotor ataxia
quotes: She was leav- ing a street car at the time of the accident
Locomotor ataxia as the result of trauma is, I believe, very rare.

modernReading.text: Tabes dorsalis (late syphilis of the spinal cord), which the fall did not cause. Early tabes was often mistaken for hysteria or injury. Absent knee jerks and pupils that do not react to light were known tests in 1896.

fixed: vague pains and weak legs months later
absent knee reflexes and unreactive pupils for a doctor who checks

constrained.rule: the past infection is unknown to the patient or not admitted

notes: A case where the obvious story (the accident) is wrong. Only an examination finds the cause.
